1079.title: A hymn in Bihagra
1079.hook: inside the Bihagra ballad, a salok headed with Mardana's name talks about wine
1079.howItsDone: The Var of Bihagra is sung in kirtan with its saloks, and Sikh scholars discuss the saloks headed with Mardana's name, reading them either as Guru Nanak's words addressed to Mardana or as Mardana's own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Bihagra, where Guru Ram Das calls his soul my dear life, and your line was night longing. A new week begins, still at night.

A wine jar, a cup, and someone drinking far too much. Not the picture one might expect inside a holy book's night raga. But there it is, in the ballad of Bihagra in the Guru Granth Sahib. Between the ballad's stanzas sit short verses called saloks, and some of them carry a heading with a name: Mardana, Guru Nanak's companion, the rabab player who traveled with him.
screen: `A WINE JAR AND A CUP.` → `A SALOK HEADED MARDANA.` → `INSIDE THE NIGHT BALLAD.`

segments.voice: The ballad is the Var of Bihagra, with stanzas by Guru Ram Das and saloks set between them. One salok, headed Mardana, paints the scene, in plain English. This dark age is the wine jar. Desire is the wine. The mind is the one drinking. Anger is the cup, filled with attachment, and pride is the one pouring. Anyone who's watched someone lose a night to drinking knows the picture: the cup keeps getting filled, and the drinker keeps reaching. The salok says the mind does the same with desire. Then it turns the picture around. Make the body the still, it says, and from it draw a different drink, one that runs like nectar. In the company of the holy, the cup becomes loving attention, filled with that nectar, and drinking it cuts the faults away. The night raga fits: the longing that might pour itself into the wrong cup is turned toward God. Now, who wrote it? The heading names Mardana along with the mark the Granth uses for Guru Nanak, and Sikh readers take that in more than one way. Some Sikh scholars read these saloks as Guru Nanak's own words, spoken to Mardana or about him. Others read the heading as giving the words to Mardana himself. The Granth doesn't stop to settle it, and neither does this lesson. Either way, a companion's name stands on the page beside the Guru's, in a ballad sung at night. The longing doesn't vanish. It finds its proper cup.
screen: `THE DARK AGE IS THE WINE JAR.` · `DESIRE THE WINE, THE MIND THE DRINKER.` · `A DIFFERENT CUP: LOVING ATTENTION.` · `MARDANA'S NAME ON THE PAGE.` · then, large: `LONGING AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Think of the last thing you reached for late at night, scrolling, snacking, one more episode, one more glass, and just see the reach, without judgment. Then ask what the reach was really for, rest, company, comfort, quiet, and hold that real wish for a moment. If you pray, offer it with Waheguru; if you don't, simply name the wish to yourself.

1080.title: Raga Vadhans
1080.hook: a raga that opens with peacocks in the rain and holds both wedding songs and laments
1080.howItsDone: Shabads in Vadhans are sung in that raga in kirtan; Guru Ram Das's ghorian are linked with wedding occasions, and Guru Nanak's alahnian, laments, are linked with mourning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Bihagra, Mardana's salok of the wine and the cup, and your line was longing at night.

Monsoon rain on a tin roof. Peacocks calling from the fields, that sharp, high cry that carries a long way. That's the first sound Raga Vadhans makes in the Guru Granth Sahib. Its opening hymn, by Guru Nanak, begins with the peacocks singing and a voice telling her sister that the rainy season of Sawan has come. Joy, color, wet earth. And yet, further into the same raga, there are songs for a wedding and songs for the dead, side by side.
screen: `PEACOCKS IN THE RAIN.` → `SISTER, SAWAN HAS COME.` → `WEDDINGS AND MOURNING.`

segments.voice: Start with the peacocks. In the opening hymn of Vadhans, in plain English, the peacocks call sweetly: sister, the rainy season has come. In this hymn the rains are the season of love; the bride hears them and thinks of her Husband Lord. It's yesterday's longing, but the night has given way to rain and color. Now turn the pages. Later in Vadhans, Guru Ram Das wrote ghorian, songs of the wedding horse. In Punjabi custom, ghorian are sung as the groom sets out on his mare, and the Guru's ghorian take that joyful scene and make it about the soul riding toward God. Further on, Guru Nanak wrote alahnian, laments, the songs of mourning sung for the dead. A wedding and a funeral, in one raga. That's not a mistake in the filing. Both are moments when a life crosses a threshold: a bride or groom leaving one home for another, a soul leaving this world. The Gurus set both to the same music. The raga doesn't pick a side between joy and grief; it holds them both. And the Granth turns both toward God. The wedding becomes the soul's union with the Lord. The lament sets the loss inside the Creator's order. Tomorrow, a closer look at one of each.
screen: `PEACOCKS, SISTER, THE RAINS HAVE COME.` · `GHORIAN: SONGS OF THE WEDDING HORSE.` · `ALAHNIAN: SONGS OF MOURNING.` · `TWO THRESHOLDS, ONE RAGA.` · then, large: `JOY AND GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Open one hand and bring to mind something glad from this year, a birth, a wedding, a good day; open the other and bring to mind a loss, large or small, and let each rest where it is. Don't trade one for the other; just hold both, and breathe between them. If you pray, say Waheguru over both hands. If a loss feels heavier than you can hold, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

1081.title: A hymn in Vadhans
1081.hook: a wedding song about a horse and a lament that begins with praise, a few pages apart
1081.howItsDone: Guru Ram Das's ghorian and Guru Nanak's alahnian are both sung in Raga Vadhans; the ghorian are associated with weddings and the alahnian with mourning, and both turn the occasion toward remembrance of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Vadhans: peacocks in the rain, and wedding songs and laments in one raga. Your line was joy and grief.

What's the first word of a funeral song? In Guru Nanak's laments in Raga Vadhans, it's blessed. A few pages earlier in the same raga, the music is for a different scene: a horse groomed and saddled in a lane strung with lights, relatives singing, the groom climbing on, the drum starting up. Today, one song of each.
screen: `A LAMENT THAT BEGINS: BLESSED.` → `A HORSE IN A LANE OF LIGHTS.` → `ONE RAGA, BOTH SONGS.`

segments.voice: First, the wedding. Guru Ram Das's ghorian, the songs of the wedding horse, start with a surprise of their own. The horse isn't a horse. In plain English: this body is the mare, and the Lord made it. Blessed is the human body, the song says, gained by good fortune. Then it puts on the saddle of understanding what is good, and rides the mare across the hard road toward the Lord. The groom's ride to the bride's home becomes the soul's ride toward God. Anyone who has seen a groom set out has the picture already; the Guru only changes who's riding where. Now the lament. Guru Nanak's alahnian open, in plain English: blessed is the Creator, the true King, who has set the whole world to its tasks. A mourning song that starts by praising the One who made the order the death belongs to. Later the alahnian say it plainly: whoever comes must rise and go. That's not cold comfort. It sets the grief inside the Creator's order instead of outside it, so the mourners aren't left alone with it. Put the two side by side. Both are about leaving: a groom leaves to begin a household; a soul leaves this world. Both are about a journey toward the Lord. And both are sung in Vadhans. The Gurus didn't need one sound for celebration and another for loss. The same music walks with a family through both doors.

1082.title: Raga Sorath
1082.hook: the Granth praises Sorath, but only on one condition
1082.howItsDone: In kirtan, ragis sing shabads from the Sorath section of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Sorath, and the Var of Sorath, with its saloks between stanzas, is also sung or read in the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Vadhans: wedding songs and songs of mourning in one raga. Your line: the same raga for both.

A compliment with a condition attached. That's how the Guru Granth Sahib talks about today's raga. Inside the long Var of Sorath, between its stanzas, sits a short salok that names the raga itself. Sorath, it says, is always lovely. Then comes the word if. Not lovely because of its notes, or its singer, or the hour it's sung. Lovely if something is true of the person singing it. Today: Raga Sorath, and what the condition is.
screen: `A COMPLIMENT WITH A CONDITION.` → `SORATH IS ALWAYS LOVELY…` → `…IF.`

segments.voice: The ragas of the Granth come in a fixed order, and this path walks them two days at a time. Sorath follows Vadhans. Its pages hold hymns by several of the Gurus and by Bhagats whose words the Gurus set beside their own, and then a Var, a ballad of stanzas with saloks between them. Tradition links Sorath with steady faith; teachers describe raga moods in different ways, so hold that as tradition, not as a rule written in the Granth. Now the salok. In paraphrase: Sorath is always lovely if the true one dwells in the mind. It goes on with plain pictures of a clean mouth and an honest tongue, a person whose speech and heart match. A raga is a mood made of sound. You could sing Sorath perfectly, every note in place, and by this verse's measure it wouldn't yet be lovely. The singer finishes the song, with what lives in the mind while the mouth makes music. And steady faith? A mood that lasts only as long as the song isn't steady. The salok asks for something that stays put when the music stops: the true one held in the mind, always. Sorath sada suhavani, always lovely, is a big promise for a tune. The verse makes it a promise about a person. Steady faith.
screen: `SORATH FOLLOWS VADHANS IN THE BOOK.` · `HYMNS, BHAGATS, AND A VAR.` · `LOVELY IF THE TRUE ONE DWELLS IN THE MIND.` · `THE SINGER FINISHES THE SONG.` · then, large: `STEADY FAITH.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Sorath; if not, sit in the quiet. Rest on one steady thing, the breath at the tip of the nose or a single word, and when the mind wanders, come back without scolding. The music can rise and fall around you while the one thing stays; if you pray, let Waheguru be that word, and if you don't, the breath is enough.

1083.title: A hymn in Sorath
1083.hook: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn of the one who stays level, in pain and in praise
1083.howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Sorath hymns are sung in kirtan in gurdwaras and at home; this one is known by its opening words, jo nar dukh mai dukh nahi maanai.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Sorath, always lovely if the true one dwells in the mind. Your line: steady faith.

Picture a person who could look at a gold ring and a pinch of dust, side by side on a table, and see no difference worth fighting over. Not because gold is bad, or because they're careless. Because neither one can move them. A hymn in Sorath describes that person. It's by Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, mahala nine in the headings, and his hymns sit in a group of their own inside Sorath. Today: a hymn in Sorath.
screen: `A GOLD RING AND A PINCH OF DUST.` → `NEITHER ONE CAN MOVE THEM.` → `MAHALA NINE, IN SORATH.`

segments.voice: It opens: jo nar dukh mai dukh nahi maanai. In paraphrase: the person who, in pain, does not take the pain to heart. Then the list grows. Pleasure, affection and fear don't grip them. Gold looks to them like earth. Slander and praise pass over them alike, and so do greed, attachment and pride. Joy and sorrow, honor and dishonor, they hold all of it lightly. They let go of hoping and craving, and lust and anger can't get a hand on them. Again and again the list comes in pairs: pain and pleasure, praise and slander, honor and dishonor. The hymn isn't asking for someone who feels nothing. It describes someone who stands in the middle of each pair without being thrown to either end. Then the turn: such a person is the one in whose heart God dwells. And the closing picture, in paraphrase: Nanak says, the one the Guru has blessed knows this way, and blends with God the way water blends with water. Pour a cup into a river and try to find the cup. That's the calm here. Not a quiet room. A person so level that nothing pulls them out of shape, and so open that they disappear into God like water into water. The Guru set it in Sorath, the raga of steady faith. Calm in sorath.

segments.voice: Let the breath slow, and notice whatever arrives first: a sound, an ache, a thought about later. Give it one breath, without pushing it away or feeding it, then let it go on by, like a cup of water poured into a river, and meet the next thing the same way. If you pray, Waheguru can go with each one as it passes; if not, simply keep letting them pass.

1084.title: Raga Dhanasri
1084.hook: a raga of true wealth that opens with a frightened soul
1084.howItsDone: Ragis sing shabads from the Dhanasri section of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Dhanasri during kirtan, and the raga's opening hymn by Guru Nanak is sung in gurdwaras as well as read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Sorath: Guru Tegh Bahadur's level person, blending with God like water with water. Your line: calm in sorath.

Who counts as rich? A bank would answer with a number. A grandmother might answer with the people at her table. Tradition links today's raga with contentment and true wealth, so you might expect its first hymn to sound settled and full. Instead, the first voice you hear in Dhanasri is afraid. Today: Raga Dhanasri, and how a raga of true wealth starts from fear.
screen: `WHO COUNTS AS RICH?` → `A RAGA OF TRUE WEALTH.` → `ITS FIRST VOICE IS AFRAID.`

segments.voice: Dhanasri comes after Sorath in the Granth's order. Its first hymn is Guru Nanak's, and it begins, jeeo darat hai aapna. In paraphrase: my soul is afraid; to whom should I cry out? Then the hymn answers itself: I serve the one who makes pain forgotten, the giver who is always, always giving. It doesn't pretend the fear isn't there. It names it, then turns toward a giver who never runs out. Further in, a hymn of Guru Amar Das plays on the raga's name. In paraphrase: Dhanasri is known as truly wealthy when she does the True Guru's work, giving over body and mind to that service. Dhanvanti, the wealthy one, chimes with Dhanasri, and the Guru lets the two words ring together. Some readers hear the soul as a bride in her, and if so, the bride's riches aren't jewelry. They're the work she does. Side by side, the two hymns make one idea in two steps. Fear first, honestly said: I don't have enough, I can't hold this. Then a different wealth: a giver who keeps giving, and a life spent in service. Contentment follows, because a person held by an endless giver can stop counting. That's true wealth.

segments.voice: If you can, play a shabad in Raga Dhanasri, then let one worry about not having enough come up, money, time, strength or patience, and name it plainly, the way the hymn does. Then slowly count what holds you right now that you didn't earn: breath, a floor, someone who would pick up if you called. If you pray, say Waheguru after each one; if not, just keep counting.
Raga Dhanasri. The raga after Sorath, linked by tradition with contentment and true wealth, which opens with a frightened soul and finds riches in service. Today's word.
Your line: true wealth. Not what you keep, but what you're held by, and what you give. That's today.

1085.title: A hymn in Dhanasri
1085.hook: Dhanasri holds Guru Nanak's sky aarti, and near its end, the Bhagats' aartis
1085.howItsDone: Guru Nanak's gagan mai thaal is part of the Kirtan Sohila said at night and is sung in kirtan; the Bhagats' aarti hymns from the end of Dhanasri are also sung, and some Sikh congregations sing a sequence of these aartis together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Dhanasri, a raga of true wealth that opens with a frightened soul. Your line: true wealth. Today closes the week.

Aarti is a way of honoring what is dear by waving light before it: a tray of small flames, lifted and circled slowly. Back in year two, you met Guru Nanak's hymn that takes the tray and throws it wide: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon are its lamps, the stars are pearls. It lives in Raga Dhanasri. Keep turning the pages of Dhanasri to the end, and more aartis are waiting, sung by the Bhagats. Today: a hymn in Dhanasri, and the conversation its aartis have.
screen: `A TRAY OF SMALL FLAMES.` → `THE SKY IS THE PLATTER.` → `MORE AARTIS AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Start with Guru Nanak's hymn, gagan mai thaal, the sky as the platter. The wind is incense, the forests are flowers, and the whole universe is already performing the aarti. Nobody needs to light anything. Now the end of the raga, where the Bhagats' hymns sit. Ravidas, remembered by tradition as a leather worker, sings in paraphrase: your Name is my aarti and my cleansing bath. Then he takes the tray apart: your Name is the lamp, the oil, the wick; without the Name, everything else is show. Sain, remembered as a barber, prepares incense, lamp and ghee for an aarti, and says he would give himself for the Lord. Dhanna, remembered as a farmer, opens with the word aarta, which some readers hear as an aarti and others as the cry of a humble petitioner. He asks plainly for what a household needs: lentils and flour and ghee, shoes and clothes, a milk cow, a good horse, a good wife. Guru Nanak lifts the aarti to the sky. Ravidas brings it inward, into the Name. Sain holds the lamp with devotion. Dhanna sets it on the kitchen table. The Granth keeps all four voices in one raga. And the whole week ran the same way: longing at night in Bihagra, wedding and mourning in Vadhans, steady faith and calm in Sorath, true wealth in Dhanasri. One raga, many kinds of heart.
screen: `THE SKY IS THE PLATTER.` · `RAVIDAS: YOUR NAME IS MY AARTI.` · `SAIN'S LAMP, DHANNA'S KITCHEN.` · `ONE RAGA, MANY KINDS OF HEART.` · then, large: `THE SKY'S AARTI.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, let your attention move outward the way Guru Nanak's hymn does, to the light in the room and whatever sky is above the roof, then inward the way Ravidas does, to one word resting in the breath. Then set it down the way Dhanna does, on one plain thing your household needs, and let yourself want it honestly; if you pray, Waheguru can mark each step.
A hymn in Dhanasri. Guru Nanak's aarti with the sky as the platter, answered near the raga's end by the aartis of Ravidas, Sain and Dhanna. Today's word.
Your line: the sky's aarti. The platter is already lit. A week of ragas, done.
